title: A living sacrifice (Romans 12)
hookLine: rejoice with them that rejoice, weep with them that weep

cards: Your phone buzzes twice in the same hour. One friend: we're engaged! Another: my dad's in the hospital.
Two messages, two completely different rooms to walk into, and both need you. For eleven chapters, Romans has been about grace, faith and God's love.
In chapter twelve, Paul turns to what all that looks like on an ordinary day. A lot of it sounds like an answer to those two messages.

teach.b: It opens with a strange phrase, in the Douay-Rheims: "I beseech you therefore, brethren, by the mercy of God, that you present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, pleasing unto God, your reasonable service."
In Paul's world, a sacrifice was offered at an altar, and it usually died. Paul flips it: offer yourselves, but alive. Your bodies, meaning your whole selves: your hands, your time, your Tuesday.

Reasonable service, logike latreia, can mean worship that fits who you are, the worship of mind and heart. Then: don't be conformed to this world, but be made new in your mind. And Paul gets very practical.
You're one body with many members and different gifts. Let love be without pretending. Outdo one another in showing honor.
Be patient in tribulation, steady in prayer. Share with the saints in need.

teach.h: REJOICE WITH THEM, WEEP WITH THEM.
teach.b: And: "Rejoice with them that rejoice; weep with them that weep." Both halves are hard. Weeping with someone means staying in the hospital room instead of fixing things.
Rejoicing can be harder: being glad at a friend's engagement, with no envy in it, when your own life seems stalled. Paul puts them side by side as one living sacrifice.
The chapter ends: don't be overcome by evil, but overcome evil by good. A living sacrifice isn't a dramatic moment. It's showing up, again and again, in whichever room you're needed.

how: At Mass, the priest invites the people to pray that the sacrifice, his and theirs, be acceptable to God, and Catholics speak of offering their whole day, work, joys and sufferings, as a living sacrifice, often through a morning offering.

o: doing your duty at work without complaint
offering your whole self, alive, as worship
a fair wage paid for a servant's work

s: in Paul's world, sacrifices usually stayed alive
they usually died at the altar. Paul's surprise is a sacrifice that lives.
Paul says rejoice with them that rejoice
and weep with them that weep, side by side.
Romans 12 turns from teaching to daily life
after eleven chapters on grace, Paul shows what it looks like in practice.

games.q: in the same hour, one friend announces an engagement and another's father is rushed to hospital. Paul's advice?
o: focus only on the one in trouble.
rejoice with one and weep with the other.
games.why: rejoice with them that rejoice; weep with them that weep. both are part of the living sacrifice.

practice: Think of two people: one with good news right now, and one who is hurting.
Picture the first and give gladness for them some room, no comparing, setting envy down kindly if it shows up; then stay a moment with the second and what they're carrying, without rushing to fix it.
If you pray, offer your body, your time and hands, as Paul says.

wordCard.voice: Reasonable service. Paul's phrase for offering your whole self, alive, as worship: logike latreia, the worship of mind and heart. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: reasonable, fitting worship, the worship of mind and heart. Paul's name for offering yourself alive.

carryVoice: Your line: rejoice and weep with them. Both rooms need you. That's day five hundred sixty-eight.

sources.q: I beseech you therefore, brethren, by the mercy of God, that you present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, pleasing unto God, your reasonable service.
Rejoice with them that rejoice; weep with them that weep.
